subjects.project: Serve TP=2 and TP=4; explain bottlenecks; note when PP/EP helps.

topics.title: Types

subtopics.title: Tensor parallel
subtopics.text: Each GPU holds a slice of every weight matrix; results are combined with all-reduce after each layer.

subtopics.title: Pipeline parallel
subtopics.text: Layers are split into stages; micro-batches flow through the pipeline so stages work in parallel.

subtopics.title: Expert parallel
subtopics.text: Each GPU holds some experts, and tokens are sent to whichever GPU holds their chosen experts.

topics.explainer: When a model does not fit on one GPU, split it. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs and needs fast all-reduce, so keep it within an NVLink domain. Pipeline parallelism assigns layers to stages, tolerating slower links but adding bubbles. Expert parallelism places MoE experts on different GPUs with all-to-all routing. Sequence or context parallelism splits very long sequences. Large deployments combine them.

topics.title: Communication

subtopics.title: NCCL collectives
subtopics.text: NCCL provides all-reduce, all-gather and all-to-all collectives optimized for NVIDIA GPUs and networks.

subtopics.title: Topology awareness
subtopics.text: Place communicating GPUs on the fastest links (same NVLink domain, same switch).

topics.explainer: Distributed inference lives or dies on communication. NCCL provides collectives such as all-reduce and all-to-all. NVLink and NVSwitch give hundreds of GB/s inside a node or rack; InfiniBand or RoCE connect nodes at lower bandwidth. Good engines overlap communication with compute. Place tensor-parallel groups inside the fastest domain and check the topology with nvidia-smi topo -m before blaming the model.

quiz.q: Tensor parallelism shards…
choices: Matmuls across GPUs for one replica
quiz.why: TP splits layer math.

quiz.q: Pipeline parallelism tolerates slower links but adds…
quiz.why: Stages idle while waiting for micro-batches.

quiz.q: Expert parallelism mainly generates which collective?
quiz.why: Tokens are dispatched to experts on other GPUs and gathered back.

lesson.intuition: When a model is too big for one GPU, or too slow on one, you split it. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs; pipeline parallelism gives each GPU a slice of layers; expert parallelism spreads MoE experts across GPUs. Each split needs GPUs to talk, so the network (NVLink, InfiniBand) becomes part of the model's speed.
how: Tensor parallel (TP): split matrices across GPUs, with all-reduce communication every layer. Best inside a node over NVLink.
Pipeline parallel (PP): split layers into stages across GPUs or nodes; pass activations between stages.
Expert parallel (EP): place different MoE experts on different GPUs; route tokens with all-to-all communication.
Sequence/context parallel: split very long sequences across GPUs.
Combine them (e.g. TP within a node, PP across nodes) based on topology, and test collectives with NCCL tests.
lesson.example: TP communication: with TP = 8 and hidden size 8,192, each layer does two all-reduces of activations of size tokens × 8,192 × 2 bytes. For a decode batch of 64 tokens, that's 64 × 8,192 × 2 = 1 MiB per all-reduce, small enough that NVLink latency, not bandwidth, dominates. That's why TP across nodes over slower links usually hurts.
mistakes: Using tensor parallelism across nodes over slow networks.
Ignoring GPU topology, so communication crosses slow links.
Skipping NCCL bandwidth tests during bring-up.
lesson.enterprise: A team serving a 400B-class MoE model uses TP = 8 inside each 8-GPU node and expert parallelism across 4 nodes over InfiniBand, after NCCL tests showed one node with a faulty link that halved all-to-all bandwidth.
takeaways: TP inside the node, PP or EP across nodes.
Communication is part of model speed.
Test the fabric before blaming the model.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  subgraph N1[Node 1: NVLink]
    G1[GPU 1] --- G2[GPU 2]
    G2 --- G3[GPU ...8]
  end
  subgraph N2[Node 2: NVLink]
    H1[GPU 1] --- H2[GPU 2]
    H2 --- H3[GPU ...8]
  end
  N1 <-->|InfiniBand: PP / EP| N2
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: two 8-GPU nodes use NVLink internally for tensor parallelism and communicate over InfiniBand for pipeline or expert parallelism.

subjects.title: Multi-LoRA & Adapter Serving
subjects.why: Many customers, one base.
subjects.explainer:
Multi-LoRA batching hosts many adapters with request routing. Memory, hot-swap, noisy-neighbor need policy.

Common mistake: thousands of cold adapters in GPU memory. Another: no tenant rate isolation.

Adapters are first-class deployables.

resources.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
resources.why: LoRA paper: freeze base weights and learn low-rank update matrices, cutting trainable parameters by up to 10,000× with comparable quality.

resources.title: vLLM documentation
resources.why: vLLM docs (the site blocked our fetcher; content known from the project): install, OpenAI-compatible server, supported models, PagedAttention, quantization and distributed serving.

resources.title: Hugging Face PEFT docs
resources.why: Hugging Face PEFT docs: LoRA, QLoRA, prefix and prompt tuning and other adapters, with integration into Transformers and Accelerate.

resources.title: SGLang documentation
resources.why: SGLang docs: install, launch the server, the OpenAI-compatible API, RadixAttention prefix caching, structured outputs and the supported model list.

subjects.project: Serve two LoRAs on one vLLM; measure switch overhead and isolation.

topics.title: Memory & Routing

subtopics.title: Adapter footprints
subtopics.text: Adapters are usually tens of megabytes, versus gigabytes for the base model.

subtopics.title: Request routing
subtopics.text: Send requests to replicas that already have their adapter loaded to avoid load delays.

subtopics.title: Batching constraints
subtopics.text: Batching sequences with different adapters needs special kernels; adapters of different ranks may batch less efficiently.

topics.explainer: Multi-LoRA serving keeps one base model in memory and loads many small adapters. Adapters are megabytes to hundreds of megabytes each. The router sends each request to a server that has its adapter loaded; hot adapters stay in GPU memory, cold ones live in CPU or disk. Kernels such as Punica and S-LoRA batch requests with different adapters together. Quantized adapters save more memory.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Versioning
subtopics.text: Version each adapter and record which base model it was trained for.

subtopics.title: Canary
subtopics.text: Roll out a new adapter version to a small share of that customer's traffic and compare evals before switching fully.

subtopics.title: Noisy neighbor
subtopics.text: One busy adapter's traffic can slow others sharing the GPU; use per-adapter limits.

topics.explainer: Treat adapters as deployable artifacts with versions. Canary new adapters on a slice of traffic. A heavily used adapter can starve others, so enforce fairness. Keep rollback instant by retaining the previous version. Emit metrics per adapter (latency, errors, quality) so tenant-specific problems are visible. A useful rule: an adapter is a release, not a file. Give it a version, an owner, an eval report and a rollback path. Try it: serve two adapters on one base model and route by request header, watching latency per adapter.

quiz.q: Multi-LoRA aims to…
choices: Host many adapters on one base engine
quiz.why: Specialization without full replicas.

quiz.q: Multi-LoRA serving keeps…
choices: One base model plus many small adapters
quiz.why: Adapters share the base weights.

quiz.q: Cold adapters typically live in…
choices: CPU memory or disk until requested
quiz.why: Hot ones are promoted to GPU memory.

lesson.intuition: Many customers want their own fine-tuned model, but running a full copy for each is too expensive. LoRA adapters are tiny add-ons to a shared base model, so one GPU can serve hundreds of 'different' models by loading the right adapter for each request. The challenge is memory, routing and batching requests that use different adapters together.
how: Keep one base model in GPU memory and many small LoRA adapters in GPU, CPU or storage.
Route each request to a replica that has its adapter loaded (or can load it fast).
Batch requests across adapters using kernels that apply different adapters per sequence (e.g. S-LoRA/Punica-style).
Keep hot adapters in GPU memory, warm ones in CPU memory, and cold ones on disk.
Version, canary and monitor each adapter separately.
lesson.example: Adapter size: a rank-16 LoRA on the 4 attention projections of a 32-layer, 4,096-hidden model has about 16.8M parameters; in bf16 that's ≈ 34 MB. A GPU with 10 GB spare could hold about 300 such adapters, compared with one extra full 16 GB copy of the 8B base model.
mistakes: Pinning each customer to a dedicated GPU instead of sharing the base.
Random routing that loads and unloads adapters constantly.
No per-adapter metrics, so one customer's bad adapter goes unnoticed.
lesson.enterprise: A customer-support platform serves 600 customer-specific adapters on a shared 8B base. Adapter-aware routing keeps each customer's adapter on two replicas, and per-adapter evals gate every new version.
takeaways: One base, many tiny adapters.
Route by adapter to avoid thrashing.
Treat each adapter as a release.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R1[Req: customer A] --> RT[Adapter-aware router]
  R2[Req: customer B] --> RT
  RT --> REP[Replica: base model]
  REP --- AA[Adapter A: GPU]
  REP --- AB[Adapter B: GPU]
  CPU[(Warm adapters: CPU)] -.load.-> REP
  DISK[(Cold adapters: disk)] -.load.-> CPU
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: requests from customers A and B go through an adapter-aware router to a replica with the shared base model and their adapters in GPU memory; warm adapters wait in CPU memory and cold ones on disk.

case.title: Introducing Apple's On-Device and Server Foundation Models (Apple ML Research, Jun 2024)
case.summary: Apple's ~3B-parameter on-device model uses mixed 2-bit and 4-bit palettization averaging 3.7 bits per weight, at the same accuracy as the uncompressed model, and can go to 3.5 bits without significant quality loss. Task-specific LoRA adapters (rank 16, tens of MB each) are loaded dynamically on top of one base model.
case.lesson: On device, memory dictates the design. Compress the base model aggressively and specialize with small swappable adapters.

subjects.title: Weight Loading & Cold Start
subjects.why: Autoscaling LLMs fails if a new replica takes ten minutes to become ready.
subjects.explainer:
A new replica must get a node, pull an image, load tens to hundreds of GB of weights, initialize the engine and warm up. Each step can be measured and shortened. This subject covers where time goes, fast loading techniques, and how to choose between always-on, warm pools and scale-to-zero per model.

Common mistakes: pulling weights from object storage on every start; huge images with weights baked in and no layer caching; autoscaling on signals that react too late for a minutes-long cold start.

resources.title: vLLM Run:ai Model Streamer
resources.why: vLLM docs for Run:ai Model Streamer (site blocked our fetcher): stream safetensors weights from object storage concurrently into GPU memory to cut cold-start time.

resources.title: safetensors docs
resources.why: safetensors docs: a safe (no pickle code execution), zero-copy, memory-mappable tensor format. Why it is the default for model weights.

resources.title: Knative scale to zero
resources.why: Knative scale-to-zero docs: how idle services scale to zero, the activator and the grace-period settings that drive cold starts.

resources.title: KServe docs
resources.why: KServe: Kubernetes-native model serving with standardized protocols for predictive and generative AI, autoscaling and scale-to-zero.

subjects.project: Measure each cold-start phase for a 7B-70B model: node ready, image pull, weight load (object store vs local NVMe vs streamer), engine init, first token. Then cut total time by at least half and document which change mattered most.

topics.title: Where the Time Goes
topics.explainer: Break cold start into phases and time each: node provisioning (cloud can take minutes), image pull (CUDA images are often 10+ GB), weight download and load into GPU memory (model bytes ÷ bandwidth), engine initialization (KV cache allocation, CUDA graph capture, kernel compilation such as torch.compile), and warmup requests. Without measurement, teams optimize the wrong phase. Log timestamps for each phase on every start and keep the distribution, not just one run.

subtopics.title: Weight transfer and load
subtopics.text: Weights for large models are tens to hundreds of gigabytes; download speed often dominates cold start.

subtopics.title: Engine init and CUDA graphs
subtopics.text: Engines capture CUDA graphs and run warmup requests, which can take a minute or more.

topics.title: Fast Loading Techniques
topics.explainer: Shorten the big phases. Keep weights on node-local NVMe or a shared high-throughput cache rather than object storage. Use safetensors so tensors can be memory-mapped and streamed. Stream tensors concurrently straight to GPU memory. Pre-shard checkpoints to your tensor-parallel layout so each GPU reads only its slice. Keep images slim and pre-pulled on nodes; use lazy-loading image formats. Cache compiled artifacts (CUDA graphs, compile caches) where your engine supports it.

subtopics.title: Local NVMe and caches
subtopics.text: Cache model weights on local NVMe so new replicas don't download them over the network.

subtopics.title: safetensors and mmap
subtopics.text: safetensors files can be memory-mapped and loaded quickly and safely, unlike pickle-based formats.

subtopics.title: Image slimming and pre-pull
subtopics.text: Smaller container images and pre-pulling them onto nodes cut startup time.

topics.title: Scale-to-Zero vs Warm Pools
topics.explainer: Every model needs a readiness policy. Hot models stay always-on with headroom. Warm models keep a small pool of ready replicas and scale out from there. Cold models scale to zero and accept a first-request delay, shown honestly in the UI. Scale on leading signals (queue depth, request rate trends) and pre-scale for known peaks. For multi-model platforms, multiplex many rarely used models or LoRA adapters on shared replicas instead of dedicating GPUs to each.

subtopics.title: Hot / warm / cold tiers
subtopics.text: Hot replicas serve now, warm ones have weights cached and start fast, cold ones start from scratch.

subtopics.title: Leading autoscale signals
subtopics.text: Queue depth and request rate rise before GPU utilization does, so scale on them.

quiz.q: Time to load 140 GB of weights at 7 GB/s is about…
quiz.why: 140 ÷ 7 = 20 seconds.

quiz.q: Pre-sharding checkpoints to the TP layout helps because…
choices: Each GPU reads only its slice
quiz.why: Less data per GPU, loaded in parallel.

quiz.q: Scale-to-zero is a good fit for…
choices: Rarely used models where a first-request delay is acceptable
quiz.why: Savings outweigh occasional cold starts.

quiz.q: Why is safetensors faster to load than pickle checkpoints?
choices: It can be memory-mapped without code execution
quiz.why: Raw tensor layout enables zero-copy mapping.

lesson.intuition: Autoscaling a normal web service takes seconds. A new LLM replica can take many minutes: get a GPU node, pull a large container, copy tens of gigabytes of weights, load them onto the GPU and warm up the engine. If you only scale when the queue is already long, users wait. Cold-start work shrinks each phase and keeps some capacity warm.
how: Time each phase: node provisioning, image pull, weight download, load to GPU, engine init (CUDA graphs, warmup).
Cut image size and pre-pull images on GPU nodes.
Cache weights on local NVMe or a fast shared store; use safetensors with memory mapping and parallel streaming to GPU.
Keep warm pools or scale-to-zero only for low-priority models; scale on leading signals (queue depth, request rate) and schedules.
Show users a loading state when a cold model must start.
lesson.example: Phase budget: node 180 s + image pull 120 s + 140 GB weights at 1 GB/s from object storage 140 s + GPU load 40 s + init 60 s = 540 s (9 minutes). With pre-pulled images (0 s), weights on local NVMe at 5 GB/s (28 s) and a warm node pool (0 s), it's 28 + 40 + 60 ≈ 128 s, about 2 minutes.
mistakes: Measuring only total startup time, not each phase.
Autoscaling on GPU utilization, which reacts too late.
Huge container images that bundle weights and tools nobody uses.
lesson.enterprise: An AI search company keeps one warm replica per popular model, pre-scales before known daily peaks, and caches weights on node-local NVMe. New replicas are ready in under 2 minutes instead of 10, and peak queue times dropped sharply.
takeaways: Measure every startup phase.
Move weights close to the GPU and load in parallel.
Scale on leading signals and keep a warm pool.
lesson.diagram:
gantt
  title Cold start phases (seconds)
  dateFormat X
  axisFormat %s
  section Before
  Node        :0, 180
  Image pull  :180, 300
  Weights     :300, 440
  GPU load    :440, 480
  Init        :480, 540
  section After
  Weights NVMe :0, 28
  GPU load     :28, 68
  Init         :68, 128
lesson.diagramAlt: Gantt chart: cold start before optimization takes 540 seconds across node, image, weights, load and init; after optimization it takes 128 seconds.

subjects.title: LLM Gateways & Inference Routing
subjects.why: Routing decides cost, latency and resilience before a single token is generated.
subjects.explainer:
Gateways give every app one endpoint with keys, budgets, policy and traces, and route across providers, models and replicas. Inside a self-hosted fleet, KV- and prefix-aware routing can cut prefill work dramatically. This subject covers gateway functions, endpoint picking, and multi-model policies.

Common mistakes: round-robin across LLM replicas; fallbacks to models never evaluated with your prompts; gateways without per-tenant budgets.

resources.title: Gateway API Inference Extension
resources.why: Gateway API Inference Extension: Kubernetes-native, model-aware routing (InferencePool, endpoint picker) using KV-cache and queue-depth signals.

resources.title: LiteLLM docs
resources.why: LiteLLM docs landing page: choose between the Python SDK and the proxy, with quick start and installation.

resources.title: Envoy AI Gateway
resources.why: Envoy AI Gateway: an open-source control plane for LLM and agent traffic on Envoy, with provider routing, token rate limits and MCP support.

resources.title: llm-d
resources.why: llm-d: Kubernetes-native distributed inference (vLLM plus inference-aware routing, P/D disaggregation and KV-cache management).

resources.title: NVIDIA Dynamo (GitHub)
resources.why: NVIDIA Dynamo: a datacenter-scale distributed inference framework with disaggregated serving, KV-aware routing and multi-tier KV cache.

subjects.project: Put LiteLLM or Envoy AI Gateway in front of two self-hosted replicas and one external provider. Add per-team budgets and a fallback. Then compare round-robin against prefix-aware routing on a workload with a shared 4k-token system prompt, measuring TTFT and GPU prefill time.

topics.title: Gateway Functions
topics.explainer: A production gateway terminates auth, maps virtual keys to provider keys, enforces rate limits and budgets per team, normalizes request formats, runs policy hooks (PII redaction, injection screening, content rules), applies retries, fallbacks and hedging, and emits traces with tokens and cost. It is also where you implement model aliases ('support-default' points to a specific model version) so apps never hard-code model names.

subtopics.title: Virtual keys and budgets
subtopics.text: Virtual keys map to teams or apps, each with its own budget and allowed models, without sharing provider keys.

subtopics.title: Retries, fallbacks, hedging
subtopics.text: Retries handle transient errors, fallbacks switch models or providers, and hedging sends duplicates to cut tail latency.

topics.title: KV- and Prefix-Aware Routing
topics.explainer: LLM replicas are stateful: each holds a KV cache. A smart endpoint picker scores replicas on queue length, KV utilization, loaded LoRA adapters and prefix-cache affinity, sending requests that share a prefix to the replica that already cached it. This avoids recomputing long system prompts and documents. Balance affinity with load to avoid hot spots. The Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension standardizes this pattern; llm-d and Dynamo implement it with cache-aware schedulers.

subtopics.title: Why round-robin fails
subtopics.text: Round-robin ignores how busy each replica is and where cached prefixes live.

subtopics.title: Prefix-cache affinity
subtopics.text: Send requests with the same prefix to the same replica so its KV cache can be reused.

topics.title: Multi-Model & Multi-Provider Policy
topics.explainer: Routing policy decides which model serves a request: by tier, task, cost budget, region or a learned difficulty score. Fallback chains handle provider outages and rate limits. Every target in a chain must be evaluated with your prompts, or failover silently lowers quality. Log the routing decision with each request so cost and quality can be attributed. Review policies regularly as prices and models change.

subtopics.title: Tier and task routing
subtopics.text: Send each request to a model tier based on task type and customer tier.

subtopics.title: Fallback chains
subtopics.text: If the first model fails or is overloaded, try a predefined list of alternatives.

subtopics.title: Eval parity for fallbacks
subtopics.text: Run the same eval on primary and fallback models so you know how much quality drops during a failover.

topics.title: Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension and llm-d
topics.explainer: The Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension adds model-aware routing to standard gateways: an InferencePool groups model-server pods, and an endpoint picker chooses a pod using live signals such as queue depth, KV-cache utilization and loaded LoRA adapters. llm-d builds on vLLM and this extension for distributed inference on Kubernetes, adding prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV cache offloading. Databricks AI Gateway and similar products provide the higher-level policy layer.

subtopics.title: InferencePool and endpoint picker
subtopics.text: An InferencePool groups model-server pods; the endpoint picker chooses one per request using live metrics.

subtopics.title: Queue- and KV-aware scheduling
subtopics.text: Route requests to the replica with the shortest queue or the most reusable KV cache.

subtopics.title: Policy gateways (Databricks AI Gateway) vs inference routers
subtopics.text: Policy gateways handle auth, budgets and logging; inference routers optimize placement on replicas.

quiz.q: Prefix-aware routing saves mainly…
choices: Prefill compute for shared prompt prefixes
quiz.why: Cached KV for the prefix is reused.

quiz.q: Model aliases in a gateway let you…
choices: Swap the underlying model without app changes
quiz.why: Apps call a stable name.

quiz.q: A fallback model that was never evaluated with your prompts risks…
quiz.why: Prompts tuned for one model may fail on another.

quiz.q: Why is round-robin a poor fit for LLM replicas?
choices: It ignores KV state, queue depth and cached prefixes
quiz.why: Replicas are stateful and unevenly loaded.

lesson.intuition: An inference gateway decides where every request goes before a single token is generated. At the business level it routes between providers and models with keys, budgets and fallbacks. At the cluster level it picks the replica that will answer fastest, using signals like queue length, free KV cache, cached prefixes and loaded LoRA adapters. Round-robin ignores all of that.
how: Normalize request formats and authenticate with virtual keys tied to budgets.
Apply policy: allowed models per team, PII hooks, model aliases.
Choose model and provider by tier and task, with fallback chains that have similar eval quality.
Inside the cluster, score replicas on queue depth, KV utilization, prefix-cache match and adapter availability.
Log every routing decision for debugging and policy review.
lesson.example: Prefix-aware routing: 4 replicas serve 200 customers, each with a 6,000-token prefix (its documents and instructions). With round-robin, every replica must hold every prefix: 200 × 6,000 = 1.2M tokens of KV per replica, more than fits (say 400,000 tokens), so prefixes are evicted and recomputed constantly. Routing each customer to one home replica means each replica holds only about 50 prefixes (300,000 tokens), which fits, so most requests skip most of their prefill. Hot customers are spread across two replicas to avoid hot spots.
mistakes: Round-robin balancing that destroys cache locality.
Fallback models never evaluated against the primary.
No logs of why a request went where it did.
lesson.enterprise: A platform running llm-d on Kubernetes uses the Gateway API Inference Extension so an endpoint picker chooses pods based on queue depth and KV-cache state. Under the same load, p95 TTFT dropped about 40% compared with plain round-robin.
takeaways: Route on real-time engine signals, not round-robin.
Fallbacks need eval parity.
Log routing decisions.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> GW[Gateway: keys, budgets, policy]
  GW --> TIER{Model tier}
  TIER --> POOL[Inference pool]
  POOL --> EPP[Endpoint picker: queue, KV, prefix, LoRA]
  EPP --> P1[Pod 1]
  EPP --> P2[Pod 2]
  EPP --> P3[Pod 3]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a client calls the gateway, which applies keys, budgets and policy, chooses a model tier and an inference pool, where an endpoint picker selects a pod based on queue, KV cache, prefix and LoRA signals.

case.title: Navigating the LLM Landscape: Uber's Innovation with GenAI Gateway (Uber Engineering, Jul 2024)
case.summary: Uber's Michelangelo team built a single GenAI Gateway, a Go service, for more than 60 LLM use cases. It mirrors the OpenAI HTTP/JSON interface while routing to external vendors and Uber-hosted models. It adds a PII redactor that anonymizes requests before they go to vendors and restores the entities afterwards, plus auth, metrics and audit logs for cost attribution. At the time of writing it served about 30 customer teams and 16 million queries per month.
case.lesson: One OpenAI-compatible front door lets you add security review, PII handling, budgets and logging once, for every team. PII redaction has latency and quality costs that you need to measure.

lesson.code:
import random
# Least-outstanding-requests routing with health checks across inference replicas.
replicas = {"r1": {"inflight": 3, "healthy": True}, "r2": {"inflight": 1, "healthy": True},
            "r3": {"inflight": 0, "healthy": False}}
def pick():
    healthy = [k for k, v in replicas.items() if v["healthy"]]
    low = min(replicas[k]["inflight"] for k in healthy)
    return random.choice([k for k in healthy if replicas[k]["inflight"] == low])
chosen = pick(); replicas[chosen]["inflight"] += 1
print("routed to", chosen)
# Prefix-aware routing goes further: send requests sharing a prompt prefix to the replica holding its KV cache.

subjects.title: GPU Kernels & Attention Impls
subjects.why: Profiles and sometimes Triton.
subjects.explainer:
FlashAttention IO-aware algorithm, GQA/MQA paths, paged kernels, MLA variants. Nsight, Triton, CUDA graphs, torch.compile.

Common mistake: 'faster' kernels ignoring numerics. Another: microbenchmarks that vanish under continuous batching.

Read the profile first.

resources.title: FlashAttention
resources.why: FlashAttention: IO-aware exact attention that tiles computation to avoid materializing the N×N matrix in HBM. Faster and linear-memory.

resources.title: FlashAttention-2
resources.why: FlashAttention-2: better work partitioning across thread blocks and warps, about 2× over v1 and approaching GEMM efficiency.

resources.title: FlashAttention GitHub
resources.why: flash-attention repo: install instructions, supported GPUs and dtypes, and the API used inside most training and serving stacks.

resources.title: Triton language
resources.why: Triton: a Python DSL for writing GPU kernels at the block level. Its tutorials go from vector add to fused softmax and matmul.

resources.title: CUDA docs
resources.why: CUDA documentation hub: programming guide, best practices, toolkit release notes (CUDA 13.x) and libraries. Look things up here when kernel- or driver-level questions come up.

subjects.project: Profile attention; write small Triton fused op; compare to PyTorch.

topics.title: Attention Kernels

subtopics.title: FlashAttention IO awareness
subtopics.text: FlashAttention reorders the attention computation to minimize reads and writes to GPU main memory.

subtopics.title: MLA variants
subtopics.text: Multi-head latent attention (used in DeepSeek models) compresses keys and values into a smaller latent, needing specialized kernels.

topics.explainer: FlashAttention computes attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip SRAM, avoiding writing the huge score matrix to HBM; it is exact, just IO-aware. GQA and MQA kernels exploit shared KV heads. Paged attention kernels read KV from scattered blocks. MLA variants decompress latent KV on the fly. Numeric modes (BF16, FP8) change speed and accuracy, and newer GPUs add special instructions for them.

topics.title: Tooling

subtopics.title: Triton
subtopics.text: Triton is a Python-like language for writing GPU kernels without raw CUDA.

subtopics.title: CUDA graphs
subtopics.text: CUDA graphs record a sequence of kernel launches once and replay it, removing CPU launch overhead.

subtopics.title: Roofline
subtopics.text: A roofline plot shows whether a kernel is limited by compute or memory bandwidth, telling you what to optimize.

topics.explainer: Profile before optimizing. Nsight Systems shows the timeline of kernels, copies and gaps; Nsight Compute digs into one kernel. Triton lets you write custom GPU kernels in Python. CUDA graphs remove CPU launch overhead, which matters a lot in decode. torch.compile fuses operations automatically. The roofline model tells you whether a kernel is limited by compute or memory bandwidth, and therefore which optimization can help.

quiz.q: FlashAttention mainly reduces…
quiz.why: IO-aware tiling cuts HBM trips.

quiz.q: CUDA graphs mainly reduce…
quiz.why: Replaying captured graphs avoids per-kernel launch cost, important in decode.

quiz.q: The roofline model tells you whether a kernel is…
quiz.why: That decides which optimizations can help.

lesson.intuition: A kernel is a small program that runs on the GPU, such as one matrix multiply or one attention step. Most LLM speedups come from better kernels that move less data between slow and fast memory. FlashAttention is the famous example: it computes exact attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory instead of writing a huge score matrix to slow memory.
how: Profile first (Nsight Systems/Compute, PyTorch profiler) to see which kernels take the time.
Use a roofline view: is the kernel limited by compute or by memory bandwidth?
Use optimized implementations: FlashAttention, paged attention kernels, fused ops.
Reduce launch overhead with CUDA graphs and torch.compile.
Write custom kernels (e.g. in Triton) only when profiling shows a clear win.
lesson.example: Why FlashAttention helps: for one head with sequence length 8,192, the full attention score matrix has 8,192² ≈ 67M entries; in fp16 that's ≈ 134 MB written and read per head per layer. FlashAttention never stores it, processing tiles in on-chip SRAM and keeping running softmax statistics, so memory traffic grows roughly linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, while computing the same result.
mistakes: Optimizing kernels before profiling.
Comparing kernels at batch sizes or sequence lengths you don't use.
Ignoring numeric differences between precision modes.
lesson.enterprise: An inference team found that 15% of decode time went to small elementwise kernels. Fusing them and capturing CUDA graphs cut per-token latency by 12% without changing the model.
takeaways: Profile, then optimize.
Memory movement is usually the bottleneck.
FlashAttention: exact attention, tiled, no big score matrix.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  HBM[(HBM: large, slow)] -->|load tile Q, K, V| SRAM[On-chip SRAM: small, fast]
  SRAM --> COMP[Scores + online softmax]
  COMP --> ACC[Accumulate output]
  ACC -->|write output only| HBM
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: FlashAttention loads tiles of Q, K and V from slow HBM into fast on-chip SRAM, computes scores with online softmax, accumulates output and writes only the output back.
lesson.code:
import math
# Online softmax (the trick inside FlashAttention): one pass, running max and running sum.
def online_softmax_dot(scores, values):
    m, s, acc = -math.inf, 0.0, 0.0
    for x, v in zip(scores, values):
        m_new = max(m, x)
        s = s * math.exp(m - m_new) + math.exp(x - m_new)
        acc = acc * math.exp(m - m_new) + math.exp(x - m_new) * v
        m = m_new
    return acc / s
scores, values = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1, 3.0], [10, 20, 30, 40]
e = [math.exp(x) for x in scores]; ref = sum(w*v for w, v in zip(e, values)) / sum(e)
print(online_softmax_dot(scores, values), ref)
assert abs(online_softmax_dot(scores, values) - ref) < 1e-9

subjects.title: Capacity Planning & SLO Engineering
subjects.why: Inference is SRE with GPUs.
subjects.explainer:
Load shapes, concurrency vs batch, autoscale signals, warm pools, admission control, shedding, fallbacks, priority lanes.

Common mistake: autoscaling on CPU while GPUs bottleneck. Another: no overload playbook.

Write runbooks while calm.

resources.title: Google SRE Book
resources.why: Free Google SRE book: SLOs, error budgets, toil, monitoring, incident management, release engineering. Read chapters 4 and 6 before running AI in production.

resources.title: vLLM documentation
resources.why: vLLM docs (the site blocked our fetcher; content known from the project): install, OpenAI-compatible server, supported models, PagedAttention, quantization and distributed serving.

resources.title: vLLM disaggregated serving guide
resources.why: vLLM blog (Sep 2026): what disaggregated serving buys you, how to run prefill/decode separation end to end in vLLM, and pitfalls.

subjects.project: Size GPUs for a latency SLO with headroom; write overload runbook.

topics.title: Planning

subtopics.title: Load shapes
subtopics.text: Look at daily and weekly patterns, bursts and prompt-length mix, not just average requests per second.

subtopics.title: Concurrency vs batch
subtopics.text: Concurrency is requests in flight; each replica has a maximum before latency targets break.

subtopics.title: Headroom
subtopics.text: Keep spare capacity for spikes and failures, because GPUs can't be added in seconds.

topics.explainer: Capacity planning starts with load shape: requests per second, input and output lengths, and how bursty traffic is. Concurrency is not batch size; many concurrent users can be served by continuous batching on few GPUs until KV memory runs out. Autoscale on queue depth or tokens in flight, not CPU. Keep warm pools because cold starts on GPUs take minutes. Hold headroom for spikes and failures.

topics.title: Degradation

subtopics.title: Admission control
subtopics.text: Reject or queue new requests when the system is full, instead of letting everyone slow down.

subtopics.title: Priority lanes
subtopics.text: Give critical or paying traffic its own queue so it isn't stuck behind bulk jobs.

topics.explainer: When demand exceeds capacity, degrade on purpose. Admission control rejects or queues requests before they hurt everyone. Shed non-critical traffic such as batch jobs first. Fall back to a smaller model for some tiers. Use priority lanes so paying or interactive users keep their SLOs. Communicate clearly during incidents, including status pages, because silent slowness erodes trust faster than an honest message.

quiz.q: Goodput emphasizes…
quiz.why: SLO-compliant useful work.

quiz.q: GPU serving should autoscale on…
choices: Queue depth or tokens in flight
quiz.why: CPU barely moves when GPUs saturate.

quiz.q: Warm pools exist because…
choices: GPU cold starts (node + image + weights) take minutes
quiz.why: Spikes cannot wait for cold capacity.

lesson.intuition: Inference capacity planning is site reliability engineering with expensive, slow-to-scale GPUs. You need to know your traffic shape, how many concurrent requests one replica can serve within your latency targets, and what you'll do when demand exceeds supply: queue, shed, downgrade or prioritize. Plan for peaks, not averages.
how: Characterize load: requests per second over the day, input/output lengths, burstiness.
Benchmark one replica: the maximum concurrency that still meets TTFT and ITL targets (goodput).
Size replicas for peak plus headroom, and set autoscaling on leading signals with warm pools.
Define degradation: admission control, priority lanes, shedding non-critical traffic, fallback models.
Prepare incident communications and practice them.
lesson.example: Little's law sizing: peak 30 requests per second, each lasting 8 s on average (prefill + 400 tokens decode), means 30 × 8 = 240 concurrent requests. If one replica meets SLOs up to 40 concurrent requests, you need 6 replicas, plus 30% headroom ≈ 8 replicas at peak.
mistakes: Sizing for average load instead of peak.
Scaling on GPU utilization, which stays high even when latency is fine or bad.
No plan for what to shed when demand exceeds capacity.
lesson.enterprise: A tax-software company plans for a peak 10× normal traffic in the last week before the filing deadline. It pre-scales by date, reserves a priority lane for paying users, and switches free users to a smaller model when queues exceed 2 seconds.
takeaways: Concurrency = arrival rate × duration.
Plan for peak with headroom.
Decide degradation before the incident.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  LOAD[Load shape] --> BENCH[Per-replica goodput]
  BENCH --> SIZE[Replicas = peak concurrency / per-replica + headroom]
  SIZE --> AS[Autoscale + warm pool]
  AS --> DEG{Over capacity?}
  DEG -->|yes| ADM[Admission control, priority lanes, fallback model]
  DEG -->|no| OK[Serve]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: load shape and per-replica goodput give a replica count with headroom, autoscaling with a warm pool, and admission control, priority lanes and fallback models when over capacity.

subjects.title: Next-Gen Hardware & Memory Systems
subjects.why: GB200-class and offload change designs.
subjects.explainer:
Blackwell/GB200, AMD MI300/ROCm, hybrid CPU+GPU, other accelerators, HBM limits, KV offload, CXL, multi-host KV.

Common mistake: interconnect-light hardware for heavy TP/EP. Another: ignoring power/cooling in BOM.

Briefs tied to traffic mix.

resources.title: CUDA docs
resources.why: CUDA documentation hub: programming guide, best practices, toolkit release notes (CUDA 13.x) and libraries. Look things up here when kernel- or driver-level questions come up.

resources.title: NCCL user guide
resources.why: NCCL overview: collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter), communicators and topology awareness across NVLink, PCIe and InfiniBand.

resources.title: TensorRT-LLM docs
resources.why: TensorRT-LLM docs: build optimized engines, quantization (FP8/INT4), in-flight batching and multi-GPU serving on NVIDIA hardware.

resources.title: vLLM documentation
resources.why: vLLM docs (the site blocked our fetcher; content known from the project): install, OpenAI-compatible server, supported models, PagedAttention, quantization and distributed serving.

subjects.project: Design brief: NVLink-heavy vs many smaller GPUs for your ISL/OSL mix.

topics.title: Platforms

subtopics.title: Blackwell/GB200 class
subtopics.text: GB200 NVL72 links 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs in one NVLink domain, acting like one large GPU for some workloads.

subtopics.title: AMD ROCm
subtopics.text: AMD Instinct GPUs use the ROCm software stack; check engine and kernel support for your models.

topics.explainer: Hardware sets serving economics. NVIDIA Blackwell and GB200 NVL72 racks connect 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, ideal for big MoE models. AMD Instinct GPUs with ROCm offer large HBM and are supported by major engines. CPU-plus-GPU superchips share memory coherently. Other accelerators (TPUs, Trainium, Gaudi, inference ASICs) can be cheaper for supported models. Power per rack is now a first-class constraint.

topics.title: Memory

subtopics.title: HBM capacity/bandwidth
subtopics.text: HBM capacity limits model and KV size per GPU; bandwidth limits decode speed.

subtopics.title: CXL pools
subtopics.text: CXL lets servers attach extra memory over a PCIe-based link, a possible tier for KV caches.

topics.explainer: HBM capacity decides how many sequences and how much context fit; HBM bandwidth decides decode speed. KV offload to CPU or NVMe and CXL memory pools extend capacity. Multi-host KV stores let any server reuse cached prefixes. Each extra tier adds latency and new failure domains, so measure hit rates before adding complexity. Try it: compute how many 8k-token sequences fit in the KV budget of your GPU, then compare with what the engine logs at startup.

quiz.q: Heavy TP across nodes needs…
quiz.why: Collectives demand fabric.

quiz.q: HBM bandwidth mostly determines…
quiz.why: Decode re-reads weights each step.

quiz.q: A GB200 NVL72 rack is notable for…
quiz.why: Large NVLink domains suit big TP and MoE.

lesson.intuition: Hardware sets the limits for inference: how much memory each accelerator has, how fast it can read that memory, how many accelerators can talk at high speed, and how much power the rack can deliver. Newer systems like NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 connect 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, and memory tiers like CPU memory and CXL change how big KV caches can get.
how: Compare accelerators on HBM capacity, memory bandwidth, low-precision compute (FP8/FP4) and interconnect.
Consider software maturity: CUDA, ROCm for AMD, and support for other accelerators in your engine.
Plan memory tiers: HBM for hot data, CPU memory or NVMe for KV offload, emerging CXL pools.
Check power and cooling: rack density can require liquid cooling.
Define failure domains: what happens when one GPU in a large NVLink domain fails.
lesson.example: Bandwidth bound on decode: a 70B model in FP8 is 70 GB. On an accelerator with 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth (Blackwell-class B200 is about 8 TB/s), a single sequence can decode at most ≈ 8,000 / 70 ≈ 114 tokens per second; on 3.35 TB/s (H100), ≈ 48 tokens per second. More bandwidth directly raises single-stream speed.
mistakes: Comparing peak FLOPs while your workload is memory-bandwidth-bound.
Ignoring software support for non-NVIDIA hardware.
Ordering high-density racks without the power and cooling to run them.
lesson.enterprise: A cloud provider tests AMD MI300X for a 70B model because its 192 GB of HBM fits the model and a large KV cache on one GPU, avoiding tensor parallelism, after confirming vLLM support on ROCm for their models.
takeaways: Memory capacity and bandwidth drive inference.
Software support is part of the hardware choice.
Power and cooling are hard limits.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TB
  HBM[HBM: fastest, smallest] --> CPU[CPU memory: larger]
  CPU --> CXL[CXL pool]
  CXL --> NVME[NVMe: largest, slowest]
  NVL[NVLink domain: many GPUs] --- HBM
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: memory tiers from fast, small HBM to CPU memory, CXL pools and slow, large NVMe, with an NVLink domain connecting many GPUs' HBM.

subjects.title: Inference Research Watchlist
subjects.why: Papers become engine features fast.
subjects.explainer:
Better speculation, learned schedulers, cross-request memory, energy-aware serving, MoE placement. Follow MLSys and engine roadmaps.

Common mistake: adopting a paper before the bottleneck matches. Another: never revisiting quarterly.

Tag reading: try/watch/ignore.

resources.title: vLLM documentation
resources.why: vLLM docs (the site blocked our fetcher; content known from the project): install, OpenAI-compatible server, supported models, PagedAttention, quantization and distributed serving.

resources.title: SGLang documentation
resources.why: SGLang docs: install, launch the server, the OpenAI-compatible API, RadixAttention prefix caching, structured outputs and the supported model list.

resources.title: PagedAttention / Efficient LLM Serving
resources.why: vLLM's PagedAttention paper: manage KV cache in fixed-size blocks like OS virtual memory, nearly eliminating fragmentation and allowing sharing. 2–4× throughput.

resources.title: DistServe Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
resources.why: DistServe: put prefill and decode on different GPUs to remove interference and optimize goodput under TTFT/TPOT SLOs.

resources.title: Speculative Decoding (Leviathan et al.)
resources.why: Leviathan et al.: a small draft model proposes tokens and the large model verifies them in parallel, with output distribution provably unchanged. 2–3× speedups.

subjects.project: Pick one recent inference paper; reproduce a figure or toy the idea.

topics.title: Active Topics

subtopics.title: Better speculation
subtopics.text: New drafters and verification schemes aim to raise acceptance rates and keep speedups at larger batch sizes.

subtopics.title: Cross-request KV
subtopics.text: Sharing or reusing KV caches across requests and nodes reduces repeated prefill work.

subtopics.title: Energy-aware serving
subtopics.text: Energy-aware serving adjusts frequency, batching and placement to cut power per token.

subtopics.title: MoE placement
subtopics.text: Deciding which experts sit on which GPUs reduces communication and load imbalance in MoE serving.

topics.explainer: Inference research moves monthly. Watch better speculation methods, learned schedulers that predict output length, cross-request KV sharing at cluster scale, energy-aware serving that trades a little latency for power, smarter MoE expert placement, and new variants of disaggregation. Before adopting a paper, check whether the gains hold at your batch sizes, models and hardware, and whether a maintained engine already implements it.

quiz.q: Before adopting a paper…
choices: Confirm it targets your measured bottleneck
quiz.why: Bottleneck fit first.

quiz.q: A paper's speedup may not transfer if…
choices: Your batch sizes, models or hardware differ
quiz.why: Gains are often regime-specific.

quiz.q: Learned schedulers try to predict…
choices: Output length or cost of requests
quiz.why: Better length estimates improve batching and fairness.

lesson.intuition: Inference research moves into production engines within months: PagedAttention, FlashAttention, speculative decoding and disaggregation all started as papers. A watchlist helps you notice ideas that matter for your workload, read them critically and test them, without chasing every new preprint.
how: Follow a few sources: engine release notes (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM), major conferences (MLSys, OSDI, NeurIPS) and arXiv.
For each idea, ask: which bottleneck does it attack (compute, memory, communication, scheduling)? Does my workload have it?
Check the evaluation setup: model sizes, sequence lengths, batch sizes and hardware.
Reproduce on your traffic shape before adopting.
Track adoption: when an engine ships it, test it behind a flag.
lesson.example: Reading a claim critically: a paper reports '3× throughput'. The fine print: batch size 1, 128-token outputs, a 7B model on one GPU. Your workload is batch 64 with 1,000-token outputs on a 70B model with TP = 4. Speculative-style gains usually shrink at large batch, so expect much less and measure before planning capacity around it.
mistakes: Adopting a technique because of a headline number from a different workload.
Ignoring engine release notes, where features land first.
Testing new features without a flag and a rollback.
lesson.enterprise: An inference team reviews new papers monthly in a 30-minute session, keeps a table of ideas mapped to bottlenecks, and runs a benchmark whenever a relevant feature lands in their engine. Prefix-aware routing and FP8 KV both went from 'watch' to production this way.
takeaways: Map each idea to a bottleneck.
Check the evaluation setup against yours.
Adopt behind flags, with benchmarks.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC[Papers + release notes] --> MAP[Map to bottleneck]
  MAP --> FIT{Matches my workload?}
  FIT -->|no| WATCH[Watchlist]
  FIT -->|yes| REPRO[Reproduce on my traffic]
  REPRO --> FLAG[Ship behind flag]
  FLAG --> PROD[Production]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: papers and release notes are mapped to bottlenecks; if they match the workload they are reproduced, shipped behind a flag and promoted to production, otherwise kept on a watchlist.

tracks.name: AI Infrastructure
tracks.role: Owns GPU platform: clusters, scheduling, storage, networking, observability, cloud. Differs from Inference (engines) and Architect (solution design).

subjects.title: GPU Architecture Literacy
subjects.why: Schedule devices you understand.
subjects.explainer:
SMs, HBM, L2, Tensor Cores, numeric formats, MIG/MPS, power/thermals. Drivers, CUDA/ROCm, container toolkits.

Common mistake: GPU util without HBM/SM clocks. Another: CUDA version skew across nodes.

nvidia-smi and DCGM are literacy.

resources.title: CUDA docs
resources.why: CUDA documentation hub: programming guide, best practices, toolkit release notes (CUDA 13.x) and libraries. Look things up here when kernel- or driver-level questions come up.

resources.title: NVIDIA GPU Operator
resources.why: NVIDIA GPU Operator docs: automates drivers, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter and MIG manager on Kubernetes nodes.

resources.title: NCCL user guide
resources.why: NCCL overview: collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter), communicators and topology awareness across NVLink, PCIe and InfiniBand.

subjects.project: Collect metrics under idle/prefill/decode loads; explain differences.

topics.title: Hardware

subtopics.title: SMs, HBM, L2
subtopics.text: SMs are the GPU's compute units; HBM is high-bandwidth memory stacked next to the chip; L2 is a shared cache between them.

subtopics.title: Numeric formats / Tensor Cores
subtopics.text: Tensor Cores perform small matrix multiplies per clock in formats like bf16, FP8 and INT8, far faster than regular cores.

subtopics.title: MIG / MPS
subtopics.text: MIG gives hardware-isolated slices (up to 7 on A100/H100); MPS shares one GPU among processes without hard isolation.

topics.explainer: A GPU is many streaming multiprocessors (SMs) sharing an L2 cache and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Tensor Cores do the matrix math, fastest in low-precision formats such as BF16, FP8 and FP4. HBM size limits what fits; HBM bandwidth limits decode speed. MIG splits one GPU into isolated slices; MPS lets processes share SMs concurrently. GPUs throttle when hot or power-capped, so clocks matter as much as utilization. Learn the failure modes too: ECC errors, fallen-off-the-bus events, and NVLink errors.

topics.title: Software

subtopics.title: CUDA / ROCm drivers
subtopics.text: The kernel driver must support the CUDA version your containers use; newer drivers generally support older CUDA runtimes.

subtopics.title: Version skew
subtopics.text: Mismatched driver, CUDA, NCCL and framework versions cause crashes or slowdowns; pin and test combinations.

topics.explainer: The software stack goes kernel driver, CUDA (or ROCm) runtime, libraries such as cuDNN, cuBLAS and NCCL, then frameworks. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit exposes GPUs to containers. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES controls which GPUs a process sees. The classic production bug is version skew: a container built for a newer CUDA than the node's driver supports, or different driver versions across nodes in one training job. Pin and inventory versions everywhere.

quiz.q: HBM bandwidth most constrains…
quiz.why: Decode streams weights/KV from HBM.

quiz.q: MIG differs from MPS in that MIG…
choices: Partitions the GPU into hardware-isolated slices
quiz.why: MIG gives dedicated SMs, memory and cache per slice.

quiz.q: A container built for a newer CUDA than the node driver supports will…
quiz.why: Driver and userspace must be compatible.

lesson.intuition: A GPU is a factory with thousands of small workers (cores grouped into streaming multiprocessors) and a very fast but limited warehouse (HBM memory). AI work is mostly huge matrix multiplications that suit those workers, and Tensor Cores are special machines for exactly that. Infra engineers need to know the parts well enough to schedule, share and troubleshoot GPUs.
how: Compute: GPUs contain many streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each with CUDA cores and Tensor Cores for matrix math.
Memory: HBM holds weights and data; an L2 cache and on-chip SRAM sit between HBM and the cores.
Number formats: Tensor Cores run fastest at low precision (bf16, FP8 and on newer chips FP4).
Sharing: MIG splits some GPUs into isolated slices; MPS lets processes share one GPU concurrently.
Software stack: driver, CUDA or ROCm runtime, libraries (cuDNN, NCCL) and the container toolkit must be version-compatible.
lesson.example: Reading a spec sheet: an H100 SXM has 80 GB of HBM3 at about 3.35 TB/s, up to 700 W, and roughly 990 dense bf16 TFLOPS (about double with structured sparsity). Its ratio of compute to bandwidth is ≈ 990e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 300 FLOPs per byte, so any kernel doing fewer than about 300 operations per byte read is memory-bound.
mistakes: Mixing driver and CUDA versions so containers fail with obscure errors.
Ignoring power and thermal limits, which throttle clocks and look like slow code.
Assuming every GPU supports MIG or every format; check the model and generation.
lesson.enterprise: A platform team standardizes on one driver version per node pool, validated with a burn-in test, and labels nodes with GPU model and MIG capability so schedulers place workloads correctly.
takeaways: SMs + Tensor Cores do the math; HBM bandwidth often sets the pace.
Lower precision = faster, if quality holds.
Keep the software stack versions aligned.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TB
  HBM[(HBM: 80 GB, ~3.35 TB/s)] <--> L2[L2 cache]
  L2 <--> SM1[SM: CUDA cores + Tensor Cores + SRAM]
  L2 <--> SM2[SM]
  L2 <--> SMN[SM ... ~132]
  DRV[Driver + CUDA + NCCL] -.-> SM1
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: HBM connects through an L2 cache to many streaming multiprocessors, each with CUDA cores, Tensor Cores and SRAM, managed by the driver, CUDA and NCCL stack.
lesson.code:
# Inspect GPUs: model, memory, utilization, topology, and ECC/XID health
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,memory.used,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv
nvidia-smi topo -m                      # NVLink / PCIe / NUMA affinity matrix
nvidia-smi -q -d ECC | grep -i -A3 "volatile"
dmesg | grep -i xid                     # XID errors point at failing hardware or drivers

subjects.title: Kubernetes for Accelerators
subjects.why: K8s + device plugins is the default platform.
subjects.explainer:
Device plugins, GPU Operator, quotas, taints/affinities, DRA. Jobs vs Deployments vs Ray. Model pull init containers; PVC vs NVMe; pod security.

Common mistake: YAML asks for 1 GPU, runtime sees 0. Another: no split between train and serve nodes.

Golden images beat snowflakes.

resources.title: Kubernetes Device Plugins
resources.why: Kubernetes device plugins: how vendors advertise GPUs (nvidia.com/gpu) to the kubelet, with the registration and allocation flow.

resources.title: NVIDIA GPU Operator
resources.why: NVIDIA GPU Operator docs: automates drivers, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter and MIG manager on Kubernetes nodes.

resources.title: K8s scheduling
resources.why: Kubernetes scheduling concepts: kube-scheduler, node affinity, taints and tolerations, pod priority and preemption. All of these matter for GPU placement.

resources.title: Ray docs
resources.why: Ray docs: Core tasks and actors, Ray Train, Serve and Data. A common substrate for distributed training, batch inference and RL.

subjects.project: Stand up GPU Operator path; schedule a CUDA job with resource requests.

topics.title: Devices

subtopics.title: Device plugins
subtopics.text: A device plugin advertises GPUs to the kubelet as extended resources and mounts them into containers.

subtopics.title: GPU Operator
subtopics.text: The NVIDIA GPU Operator automates installing drivers, container runtime hooks, the device plugin and DCGM monitoring.

subtopics.title: Taints / affinity
subtopics.text: Taints repel pods without matching tolerations; node affinity steers pods to specific GPU types.

topics.explainer: Kubernetes sees GPUs through device plugins that advertise resources like nvidia.com/gpu. The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs and manages the driver, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, MIG manager and feature discovery as one unit. Use ResourceQuotas to cap GPUs per namespace, and taints plus node affinity to keep non-GPU pods off expensive nodes. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) is the newer API for richer device requests.

topics.title: Workloads

subtopics.title: Deployments vs Jobs vs Ray
subtopics.text: Use Deployments for long-running servers, Jobs for batch tasks and Ray for distributed Python workloads.

subtopics.title: Init model pulls
subtopics.text: Init containers can download model weights before the main container starts.

subtopics.title: Priority classes
subtopics.text: Priority classes let important workloads preempt lower-priority pods when resources are short.

topics.explainer: Training fits Jobs (or JobSet, Kubeflow Training Operator, or Ray via KubeRay); serving fits Deployments behind autoscalers. Model weights are large, so pull them with init containers or sidecars, or mount a shared volume or cache to avoid every pod downloading 100 GB. EmptyDir on local NVMe is fast scratch; PVCs persist. Apply pod security standards even to GPU workloads, and use PriorityClasses so production serving can preempt experiments.

topics.title: Day-2 GPU Cluster Ops
topics.explainer: Running GPU clusters day to day means planned driver upgrades with drains, node health checks before scheduling, labeling nodes by GPU model and health, autoscaling node pools, and keeping spare capacity for failures. Track allocatable versus used GPUs per namespace to spot waste. Keep runbooks for stuck pods holding GPUs and for nodes whose device plugin stopped advertising devices. Most outages here are slow leaks, not explosions.

subtopics.title: Driver upgrade drains
subtopics.text: Cordon and drain a node, upgrade the driver, run health checks, then uncordon, one node or batch at a time.

subtopics.title: Allocatable vs used tracking
subtopics.text: Allocatable GPUs are what the scheduler can hand out; used means actually busy. A big gap means waste.

quiz.q: GPU Operator primarily…
quiz.why: Operator manages GPU software lifecycle.

quiz.q: Taints on GPU nodes are used to…
choices: Keep non-GPU pods off expensive nodes
quiz.why: Only pods tolerating the taint schedule there.

quiz.q: Init containers or node caches for model weights avoid…
choices: Every pod downloading huge weights on start
quiz.why: Weight pulls dominate cold start.

lesson.intuition: Kubernetes doesn't know what a GPU is out of the box. Device plugins and the NVIDIA GPU Operator teach it to discover GPUs, advertise them as resources, and hand them to containers. On top of that you need scheduling rules so GPU nodes run GPU work, plus day-2 operations like driver upgrades without breaking running jobs.
how: Install the GPU Operator (drivers, container toolkit, device plugin, monitoring) on GPU node pools.
Pods request GPUs with resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu: 1; the scheduler places them on nodes with free GPUs.
Use taints on GPU nodes and tolerations on GPU pods so CPU workloads don't land there; add affinity for GPU types.
Choose workload types: Deployments for serving, Jobs for batch, Ray or operators for distributed work.
Operate: quotas and priority classes, health-gated scheduling, drain-based driver upgrades, autoscaling node pools.
lesson.example: Allocatable vs used: a node pool has 10 nodes × 8 GPUs = 80 allocatable GPUs. 72 are requested by pods, so the scheduler sees 90% allocation. DCGM shows average utilization of only 35% because many serving pods sit idle at night. Allocation looks full while hardware is mostly idle, which points to sharing, autoscaling or smaller requests rather than buying more GPUs.
mistakes: No taints on GPU nodes, so CPU pods consume their memory and CPUs.
Upgrading drivers in place without draining, killing running jobs.
Measuring only allocation, not real utilization.
lesson.enterprise: A media company runs inference Deployments and nightly batch Jobs in one cluster. Priority classes let serving preempt batch during traffic peaks, and driver upgrades roll through one node at a time with automatic drain and health checks.
takeaways: GPU Operator + device plugin make GPUs schedulable.
Taints, tolerations and priorities keep GPUs for GPU work.
Track allocatable vs actually used.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 + toleration] --> SCH[Scheduler]
  SCH --> NODE[GPU node: taint gpu=true]
  NODE --> DP[Device plugin]
  DP --> GPU[GPU]
  OP[GPU Operator] -.installs.-> DP
  OP -.installs.-> DRV[Driver + toolkit + DCGM]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a pod requesting a GPU with a toleration is scheduled to a tainted GPU node, where the device plugin assigns a GPU; the GPU Operator installs the plugin, drivers, toolkit and DCGM.

case.title: Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes (Jan 2021)
case.summary: OpenAI runs large ML jobs with typically one pod per node. Healthchecks cordon bad nodes, and 'preflight' GPU tests run behind a taint before a node takes work. Team capacity is enforced with taints and tolerations. All-or-nothing gang scheduling uses the Coscheduling plugin to avoid half-scheduled deadlocks. EndpointSlices cut a major API-server load by about 1000×.
case.lesson: Accelerator clusters need health gating, gang scheduling and quota mechanisms that stock Kubernetes doesn't give you by default.

lesson.code:
# Request GPUs and land on GPU nodes (requires the NVIDIA device plugin / GPU Operator)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: llm-server}
spec:
  nodeSelector: {nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3}
  tolerations: [{key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}]
  containers:
    - name: vllm
      image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest
      args: ["--model", "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"]
      resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}}

subjects.title: Linux, Containers & Driver Ops
subjects.why: The layer that pages you.
subjects.explainer:
cgroups, hugepages, IOMMU, persistence mode, fabric manager, runtime hooks, secure base images. Debug 'GPU not found' in five minutes.

Common mistake: upgrading driver under pinned CUDA userspace. Another: writable root + host GPU in multi-tenant clusters.

Exact-command runbooks.

resources.why: Docker docs: images, Dockerfiles, Compose, BuildKit and GPU access (--gpus). The container basics behind every inference deployment.

topics.title: OS/Driver

subtopics.title: Persistence mode
subtopics.text: Persistence mode keeps the driver loaded so GPUs don't re-initialize for every new process.

subtopics.title: Fabric manager
subtopics.text: Fabric manager configures NVSwitch so GPUs in an HGX system can talk over NVLink.

subtopics.title: Driver/userspace matrix
subtopics.text: The host driver and the CUDA userspace in containers must be compatible; check NVIDIA's compatibility matrix.

topics.explainer: GPU nodes need care at the OS layer. Enable persistence mode so the driver stays loaded and first calls are not slow. NVSwitch systems require the Fabric Manager service, or multi-GPU jobs fail. Match driver and CUDA userspace per NVIDIA's compatibility matrix. IOMMU and PCIe ACS settings can silently cut peer-to-peer bandwidth. Run health checks (DCGM diagnostics) at boot and periodically to catch bad GPUs before jobs land on them.

topics.title: Containers

subtopics.title: Runtime hooks
subtopics.text: Runtime hooks from the NVIDIA container toolkit inject device files and driver libraries when a container starts.

subtopics.title: Supply scanning
subtopics.text: Scan images for known vulnerabilities and keep a software bill of materials (SBOM).

topics.explainer: Containers reach GPUs through runtime hooks (the NVIDIA Container Toolkit or CDI) that mount device files and driver libraries. Avoid privileged containers; mount only needed devices. Keep seccomp and AppArmor profiles on. Pin images by digest so a tag update cannot change your CUDA stack overnight. Scan images, since AI images are huge and pull in many dependencies. Try it: run nvidia-smi inside an unprivileged container with only the needed device mounted, and confirm it works without --privileged.

quiz.q: CUDA userspace and driver…
quiz.why: Version matrix matters.

quiz.q: NVSwitch-based servers require which service for multi-GPU jobs?
quiz.why: Fabric Manager configures the NVSwitch fabric.

quiz.q: Pinning images by digest prevents…
choices: A retagged image silently changing your stack
quiz.why: Digests are immutable; tags are not.

lesson.intuition: Under every GPU cluster is Linux: kernel modules, drivers, container runtimes and system services. This is the layer that wakes you up at night, because a missing daemon, a wrong driver version or a security profile can make a healthy-looking node useless. Knowing the basics turns mysterious failures into quick fixes.
how: Install a driver version matched to your CUDA stack, and enable persistence mode so GPUs stay initialized.
On NVSwitch systems, run the fabric manager service, or multi-GPU communication fails.
Use the NVIDIA container toolkit so the runtime mounts GPU devices and libraries into containers.
Apply security profiles (seccomp, AppArmor) and pin and scan container images.
Run health checks (nvidia-smi, DCGM diagnostics) before putting a node into service.
lesson.example: A quick health check script runs nvidia-smi to confirm 8 GPUs are visible, checks that persistence mode is on, verifies the fabric manager service is active on HGX systems, and runs a short DCGM diagnostic. Nodes that fail any step get a label that keeps the scheduler away until fixed.
mistakes: Forgetting the fabric manager on NVSwitch systems, causing NCCL failures.
Letting containers ship their own drivers that don't match the host kernel module.
Unpinned base images that change underneath you.
lesson.enterprise: A cloud GPU provider bakes a node image with a pinned driver, fabric manager and container toolkit, runs a 10-minute burn-in on every new node, and rejects nodes that fail, cutting bad-node incidents by half.
takeaways: Driver, runtime and services must match.
Health-check before scheduling.
Pin and scan images.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TB
  HW[GPU hardware] --> KM[Kernel driver module]
  KM --> SVC[Services: persistence, fabric manager]
  KM --> CT[Container toolkit hooks]
  CT --> CON[Container: CUDA userspace]
  SVC --> HC[Health checks: nvidia-smi, DCGM]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: GPU hardware is driven by a kernel module with system services and container toolkit hooks, which expose GPUs to containers; health checks run against the stack.
lesson.code:
# Run a CUDA container and verify the driver/toolkit stack end to end
nvidia-smi                                   # host driver version
docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi
cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version
lsmod | grep -E "nvidia|nvidia_uvm|nvidia_peermem"

subjects.title: Schedulers & Orchestrators
subjects.why: Scarce GPUs make policy into product.
subjects.explainer:
Slurm, Kueue, Ray/KubeRay, HPA on custom metrics. Gang scheduling, preemption, fairshare, binpacking.

Common mistake: default K8s assumptions for multi-GPU gangs. Another: train vs serve without priority.

Document the real policy.

resources.title: Slurm docs

resources.title: Kueue
resources.why: Kueue: Kubernetes-native job queueing with quotas, fair sharing and all-or-nothing admission for batch, HPC and AI workloads.

resources.title: Ray docs
resources.why: Ray docs: Core tasks and actors, Ray Train, Serve and Data. A common substrate for distributed training, batch inference and RL.

resources.title: K8s scheduling

topics.title: Batch/Train

subtopics.title: Slurm partitions/GRES
subtopics.text: Slurm partitions group nodes; GRES (generic resources) lets jobs request GPUs.

subtopics.title: Gang scheduling
subtopics.text: Gang scheduling starts all pods of a job together or none, avoiding partial allocations.

topics.explainer: Slurm still runs most HPC and many training clusters: partitions group nodes, GRES describes GPUs, and fairshare balances users. Gang scheduling starts all pods of a distributed job together or none at all, preventing deadlock where half a job holds GPUs waiting for the rest. Preemption reclaims GPUs for higher priority work, so jobs must checkpoint. Reservations hold capacity for planned runs.

topics.title: Serving

subtopics.title: HPA on tokens/s or queue
subtopics.text: Scale serving replicas on request queue length or tokens per second, which track user demand better than CPU.

subtopics.title: Kueue
subtopics.text: Kueue is a Kubernetes-native job queueing system with quotas, borrowing and preemption.

subtopics.title: Spot handling
subtopics.text: Spot GPUs are cheap but can be reclaimed; use them for checkpointed or stateless work.

topics.explainer: Serving autoscalers should scale on queue depth, tokens per second, or KV usage, not CPU. Kueue adds job queueing, quotas and fair sharing across teams on Kubernetes; Volcano offers gang scheduling and batch policies. KubeRay manages Ray clusters for serving and training. Binpacking fills nodes tightly to free whole nodes; spreading improves resilience. Spot GPUs need graceful drain and fast restart.

quiz.q: Gang scheduling is needed when…
quiz.why: Distributed barriers need co-start.

quiz.q: Kueue adds to Kubernetes…
choices: Job queueing, quotas and fair sharing
quiz.why: It admits jobs when quota is available.

quiz.q: Spot GPU serving needs…
quiz.why: Spot capacity can vanish with short notice.

lesson.intuition: When GPUs are scarce, the scheduler decides who gets to work, which makes scheduling policy a product decision. Training jobs need many GPUs at once or not at all; serving needs to scale with traffic; teams need fair shares. Different tools (Slurm, Kueue, Volcano, KubeRay) express those policies.
how: For batch and training, use gang scheduling so a job starts only when all its GPUs are free.
Set queues and fair-share policies so teams get their quota, and can borrow idle capacity.
Allow preemption: low-priority jobs yield to high-priority ones and checkpoint to resume.
For serving, autoscale on queue depth or tokens per second, not CPU.
Bin-pack small workloads to keep whole nodes free for big jobs, and handle spot interruptions.
lesson.example: Fair share: team A has a quota of 32 GPUs and team B 32 in a 64-GPU cluster. B is idle at night, so A borrows B's 32 and runs 64. At 9 a.m. B submits a job needing 16; the scheduler preempts 16 of A's borrowed GPUs (A's jobs checkpoint), giving B its share while A keeps 48.
mistakes: No gang scheduling, so jobs hold partial GPU sets and deadlock.
Static quotas with no borrowing, leaving GPUs idle.
Preempting jobs that don't checkpoint, losing hours of work.
lesson.enterprise: A research lab moved from first-come-first-served to Kueue with team quotas, borrowing and priority. Average GPU utilization rose from 55% to 80%, and urgent jobs start within minutes.
takeaways: Gang scheduling for multi-GPU jobs.
Quotas + borrowing + preemption = fairness without waste.
Autoscale serving on queue signals.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J1[Team A jobs] --> Q1[Queue A: quota 32]
  J2[Team B jobs] --> Q2[Queue B: quota 32]
  Q1 --> ADM{Admission: gang + fair share}
  Q2 --> ADM
  ADM --> CL[Cluster: 64 GPUs]
  ADM -.borrow / preempt.-> CL
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: team A and B jobs enter queues with quotas, an admission controller applies gang scheduling and fair share with borrowing and preemption, and admits jobs to a 64-GPU cluster.

case.title: Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes (Jan 2021)
case.summary: OpenAI runs large ML jobs with typically one pod per node. Healthchecks cordon bad nodes, and 'preflight' GPU tests run behind a taint before a node takes work. Team capacity is enforced with taints and tolerations. All-or-nothing gang scheduling uses the Coscheduling plugin to avoid half-scheduled deadlocks. EndpointSlices cut a major API-server load by about 1000×.
case.lesson: Accelerator clusters need health gating, gang scheduling and quota mechanisms that stock Kubernetes doesn't give you by default.

lesson.code:
# Gang scheduling: place all workers of a job or none (prevents partial-allocation deadlock).
free = {"node1": 8, "node2": 8, "node3": 4}
def gang_place(job_gpus_per_worker, workers):
    plan, avail = [], dict(free)
    for _ in range(workers):
        node = next((n for n, g in sorted(avail.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]) if g >= job_gpus_per_worker), None)
        if node is None: return None                    # do not start anything
        avail[node] -= job_gpus_per_worker; plan.append(node)
    free.update(avail); return plan
print("job A (2x8 GPU):", gang_place(8, 2))
print("job B (2x8 GPU):", gang_place(8, 2), "-> waits, holding nothing")

subjects.title: Storage for Models & Data
subjects.why: Weight distribution dominates cold start.
subjects.explainer:
Object stores, parallel FS, NVMe scratch, registries, P2P/lazy pulls, dataset streaming, index DR. Immutable versioned artifacts.

Common mistake: pulling 70B remotely on every scale-up. Another: mutable latest tags.

Cold-start budget is an SLO.

resources.title: Docker docs
resources.why: Docker docs: images, Dockerfiles, Compose, BuildKit and GPU access (--gpus). The container basics behind every inference deployment.

resources.title: Databricks ML
resources.why: Databricks' AI platform overview: building, deploying, evaluating and governing agent systems on lakehouse data (Mosaic AI, Unity Catalog).

resources.title: Google SRE Book
